notes: \cpara{Sets up a personal case. The post dates from November 2008, eight months after the posts around it; the book places it here as an everyday example of the Mind Projection Fallacy.}
\cpara{Describes the problem: the author can persist for seconds or for years, but not for hours, and advice has helped mainly by showing that other creative professionals have the same trouble.}
\cpara{The dialogue, which the author flags as ``a very loose gist''.}
\cpara{The author's habit: browsing and short videos.}
\cpara{The friends' advice, as reported, is conditional: ``if you know you can't work for a while''.}
\cpara{The author's reason for short activities: the ability to work might return at any time, unpredictably.}
\cpara{Names the assumption: the work cycle was treated as chaotic, though never called that.}
\cpara{The inference is the author's. A conditional (``if you know'') does not say that other people do know; the post marks this with ``seemed to be implying''.}

\cpara{Applies the Mind Projection Fallacy to the case. The application fits the sense Jaynes gave the term, as the author described it in ``Mind Projection Fallacy'': treating a state of partial knowledge as a property of the thing itself.}
\cpara{The alternative, hedged with ``Maybe'': the unpredictability may be in the author's predictions, not in the work cycle.}

\cpara{``Inverted stupidity'' appears nowhere else in the book, and the post does not say where it has been used ``for high abstract things like Artificial Intelligence''. The reader has to infer the meaning: one's own ignorance, seen as disorder in the world.}

\cpara{The one general claim about people, that we fail to consider our own ignorance because ``we don't think of ourselves at all''. It is marked ``I suspect'', and the post offers only the author's case for it.}

\cpara{Claims no result: the reframing does not fix the problem, and ``Saying `I'm ignorant' doesn't make you knowledgeable.'' The post was written soon after the realization and reports no test of it.}
\cpara{Ends on the modest claim that the new description at least points somewhere different.}
